chunks: My father narrated (may God be pleased with him) who said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) that he said:

The moon was withheld from the Children of Israel, so God, may His Majesty be Exalted, revealed to Moses (peace be upon him): 'Take out the bones of Joseph from Egypt.' He promised him that the moon would rise when he took out his bones. Moses asked about who knew his location, and it was said to him: 'Here is an old woman who knows of him.' So he sent for her, and a crippled, blind old woman came to him. He said to her: 'Do you know the location of Joseph's grave?' She said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then inform me of it.' She said: 'Not until you give me four things: you free my legs, you restore my youth to me, you restore my sight to me, and you make me with you in Paradise.' He said: 'That seemed great to Moses, so God, may His Majesty be Exalted, revealed to him: 'O Moses, give her what she asked, for you are only giving on My behalf.' So he did, and she showed him to it, and he took it out from the bank of the Nile in a marble coffin. When he took it out, the moon rose. They carried it to Syria, and for that reason the People of the Book carry their dead to Syria.
ai.seo_question: What were the four conditions the old woman demanded from Prophet Moses to reveal the location of Joseph's bones?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Al-Khisal* highlights the miraculous intercession of Prophet Joseph’s bones, linking their retrieval to the restoration of lunar light for the Children of Israel, a theme resonating with the 'splitting of the moon' in Islamic eschatology. The old woman’s four conditions—particularly entry into Paradise while still alive—underscore the Shia emphasis on the merit of the righteous and the tangible rewards of faith. The conclusion connecting this event to the burial customs of the People of the Book in Syria provides a historical bridge between biblical tradition and Islamic practice.
